summary: German links a subject to what it is with the verb sein (to be), and it can never be left out: Ich bin Lehrer. Er ist hier. sein is the most irregular verb of the language – bin, bist, ist, sind, seid, sind – and the first table to know by heart. With a job, a role or a nationality German uses no article: Ich bin Lehrerin (not *eine Lehrerin), Er ist Student. After das the verb agrees with what follows: Das ist ein Tisch, but Das sind Kinder and Das bin ich.

blocks.title: No article with jobs
blocks.text: Ich bin Lehrer. Sie ist Studentin. Wir sind Schüler. An article comes only with an adjective or a specific person: Er ist ein guter Lehrer. Das ist der Lehrer.

blocks.title: Man or woman?
blocks.text: The job word follows the person: Er ist Lehrer – Sie ist Lehrerin; Ich bin Student (a man) – Ich bin Studentin (a woman).

blocks.title: Das ist / Das sind / Das bin ich
blocks.text: In pointing sentences the verb agrees with the noun or pronoun after it: Das ist ein Kind. Das sind Kinder. Das bin ich. Das sind wir.

items.title: Arabic, Hebrew
points: the two nouns simply stand side by side

askYourself: Who or what is the subject? → ich bin, du bist, er/sie/es ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie/Sie sind.
Is the complement a job, role or nationality without an adjective? → no article (Ich bin Lehrer).
Is the subject a woman or a girl? → the feminine job word (Lehrerin, Studentin, Schülerin).
Does the sentence start with Das and a plural or a pronoun follows? → Das sind Kinder / Das bin ich.
Is it a yes/no question? → sein comes first: Bist du Student?
steps: Add the complement (job without article, place, or a noun with its article).

traps: *Ich bin ein Lehrer – with a job German uses no article (unless an adjective comes in: ein guter Lehrer).
ihr seid (you are) vs seit (since): same sound, different spelling.
Das sind Freunde, not *Das ist Freunde.
wir sind, sie sind and Sie sind are the same form – the pronoun decides the meaning.
Feeling cold or bad uses the dative, not “I am”: Mir ist kalt (Ich bin kalt = I am a cold person).

seeAlso.note: Arabic has no “to be” in the present: huwa ṭālib (he student); kāna appears in the past and future.
Hebrew has no present “to be” either: hu student (he student); haya / hayta in the past.
Chinese 是 links two nouns (我是老师), but an adjective needs no 是 (他很高).
The form of sein depends on the subject pronoun.

notes.text: είμαι is never left out, and a job takes no article: Είμαι δάσκαλος – Ich bin Lehrer.
Russian has no present-tense “to be” (я студент); German always needs it: Ich bin Student. The job without an article is the same.
One verb, sein, covers ser and estar: Ich bin Lehrer, Ich bin müde, Ich bin hier. As in Spanish, a job takes no article (Soy profesor – Ich bin Lehrer).
English needs “a” with a job (I am a teacher); German has none: Ich bin Lehrer. Ich bin ein Lehrer sounds wrong unless an adjective comes in (ein guter Lehrer).
Like être, sein is never left out, and a job takes no article: Je suis professeur – Ich bin Lehrer.

The copula is always there and agrees with the person (maĩ śikṣak hū̃, vah śikṣak hai), as sein does (ich bin, er ist); but German puts it second, not at the end. The speaker’s sex never shows: ich bin müde for everyone, where Hindi says maĩ thakā hū̃ / maĩ thakī hū̃.
Persian also needs “to be” (man dānešju hastam / dānešju-am); German uses a separate, very irregular verb (bin, bist, ist) and puts it second, not at the end.
āhe is always there (mī śikṣak āhe), as sein is; German puts it second and changes it for the person: ich bin, du bist, er ist.
In the present Arabic simply puts the two nouns side by side (ana ṭālib); German never does: Ich bin Student.

Hebrew has no present-tense “to be” (ani student; ha-bayit gadol); German always needs sein: Ich bin Student. Das Haus ist groß. Nothing shows the speaker’s sex: ich bin müde for ani ayef and ani ayefa alike.
Turkish adds a personal suffix (öğretmenim) and often nothing in the 3rd person (O öğretmen); German needs a separate verb in every person: Ich bin Lehrer, Er ist Lehrer.
desu / da links nouns (gakusei desu), but adjectives inflect on their own (takai); German uses sein for both: Ich bin Student. Das ist teuer.
The copula -ida is attached to the noun (haksaeng-ida), and adjectives are verbs (keuda); German has the separate verb sein for both: Ich bin Student. Das Haus ist groß.
olla is always there and a job takes no article: Olen opettaja – Ich bin Lehrer.
The 3rd person drops the copula (Anna tanár), the others keep it (tanár vagyok). German never drops it: Anna ist Lehrerin.
ni links two nouns (Mimi ni mwalimu), but it never changes; German sein changes for every person: ich bin, du bist, er ist.
是 links two nouns (我是学生), but an adjective follows without it (我很好). German uses sein in both: Ich bin Student. Mir geht es gut / Das ist gut.
là links nouns (tôi là giáo viên), but adjectives need no copula (tôi mệt); German says Ich bin müde.
Inuktitut turns the noun itself into a verb with a suffix meaning “be” and adds the person ending, all in one word. German uses the separate verb sein and a noun after it: Ich bin Lehrer.
